Leases made according to the 1938 Mineral Leasing Act are subject to regulations and approval of the Department of Interior. Regulations of Interior applying the 1938 Mineral Leasing Act to Crow coal are published in the Code of Federal Regulations at 25 CFR171, and 177; Regulations issued May 11, 1976 under 30CFR211 do not apply to operations and reclamation on Indian lands except as may now or in the future be provided in separate regulations to be issued by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. It is anticipated that the new BIA regulations will make the operating and reclamation standards contained in 30CFR211.40 applicable.
The Conservation Division, U.S. Geological Survey, approves and supervises all mineral operations on Indian Lands. Normally it also advises the agency issuing leases that certain stipulations and operating orders be included as a condition of the lease.
The U.S. Geological Survey supervises and approves the exploration plan and the mining plans. Prior to approval any necessary environmental statements are prepared and specific procedures for use in operations are delineated. Operations are periodically inspected for compliance with the approved mining plan and should conditions indicate, additional procedures can be required.
U.S. Geological Survey is also responsible for insuring that public health and safety are protected in the conduct of mining operations.

Other agencies (MESA, OSHA, etc.) are responsible for employee safety measures, as distinguished from public aspects.
The Environmental Protection Agency regulates effluent discharges into navigable waters of the United States as well as discharges of hazardous substances. The Environmental Protection Agency also regulates air quality.
